items.title: China developing mini hypersonic missiles for naval guns

featured_image.name: China is developing mini hypersonic glide missiles that can ...

items.description:
Chinese scientists and engineers have developed an ultra-small hypersonic glide missile designed to be fired from 80mm naval anti-aircraft guns, a technology that defense analysts say could fundamentally alter naval air defense if successfully deployed.

According to reporting from the South China Morning Post, the projectiles can reach speeds close to Mach 6 upon leaving the barrel, far exceeding the velocity of conventional anti-aircraft shells. This extreme speed enables the missiles to strike fighter jets or drones at ranges exceeding 20 kilometers and altitudes of approximately 10,000 meters.[1][2][3]

items.title: Japanese researchers unveil 3D framework for green ammonia production

featured_image.name: Hidden copper switch supercharges green ammonia production ...

items.description:
Scientists in Japan and the United States have developed new approaches to convert nitrate pollution into ammonia, offering potential alternatives to the century-old Haber-Bosch process that currently accounts for roughly 2% of global greenhouse gas emissions.[1][2]

Researchers at Tohoku University unveiled a three-dimensional covalent organic framework, dubbed TU-82, that achieved an 88.1% Faradaic efficiency for electrochemical nitrate-to-ammonia conversion, with an ammonia yield rate of 2.87 milligrams per hour per square centimeter. The findings, published February 2 in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A, represent the first deployment of 3D COFs for this reaction, moving beyond the two-dimensional architectures that have dominated the field.[3][4][5]

items.title: US accuses China of secret 2020 nuclear test, monitor finds no evidence

featured_image.name: U.S. accuses China of secret nuclear testing as it calls for ...

items.description:
The United States accused China on Friday of carrying out a covert nuclear test in 2020, an allegation Beijing rejected as Washington pushed for a new arms control framework following the expiration of the last remaining nuclear treaty between the US and Russia.

Thomas DiNanno, Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, made the accusation at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, one day after the New START treaty expired, marking the first time in over fifty years that the world's two largest nuclear powers operate without binding limitations on their strategic arsenals.

items.title: Cuba adopts four-day work week amid deepening energy crisis

featured_image.name: Trump says Mexico will stop sending oil to energy-starved Cuba

items.description:
Cuba announced emergency fuel-rationing measures on Friday, including a four-day work week for state companies and restrictions on fuel sales, as the island nation struggles with its worst energy crisis in years, fueled in part by President Donald Trump's executive order threatening tariffs on any country that supplies oil to Havana.

Deputy Prime Minister Oscar Perez-Oliva Fraga blamed Washington for the crisis, telling state television the government would "implement a series of decisions, first and foremost to guarantee the vitality of our country and essential services, without giving up on development."[1][2]

items.title: Mexico to send humanitarian aid to Cuba by Monday

featured_image.name: Mexico's Sheinbaum aims to send humanitarian aid to Cuba by ...

items.description:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Friday that her government will dispatch humanitarian aid to Cuba by Monday, offering food and basic supplies while diplomatic talks continue over resuming oil shipments that were suspended under pressure from the Trump administration.

"We are planning to send this aid either this weekend or on Monday at the latest," Sheinbaum said at her daily morning press conference in Mexico City. "It primarily consists of food and other supplies they have requested."[1][2]

The announcement comes as Mexico navigates a delicate diplomatic balancing act, seeking to maintain solidarity with the Cuban people while avoiding threatened tariffs from Washington. "Obviously, we do not want sanctions against Mexico, but we are in the process of dialogue and, for now, humanitarian aid will be sent," Sheinbaum stated.[2][1]

items.title: Mexico to send humanitarian aid to Cuba by Monday

featured_image.name: Mexico's Sheinbaum aims to send humanitarian aid to Cuba by Monday

items.description:
As rolling blackouts leave millions of Cubans without power and public buses grind to a halt, the United States is intensifying its pressure campaign on the island nation with executive actions targeting its already dwindling fuel supplies.

President Donald Trump's January 29 executive order declared Cuba an "unusual and extraordinary threat" to U.S. national security, authorizing tariffs on imports from any country that supplies oil to the Caribbean nation. The move has effectively severed Cuba from its remaining energy lifelines, compounding a humanitarian crisis that the United Nations warned could lead to outright "collapse."[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: US and Russia agree new nuclear talks needed after treaty expires

featured_image.name: Amid tensions, US and Russia hold ‘substantive’ arms talks

items.description:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared on Friday that any future nuclear arms control agreement must include China, announcing the Trump administration would not pursue a new bilateral deal with Russia following the expiration of the New START treaty.

In an essay published on the State Department's Substack page, Rubio argued that China's "rapid and opaque" nuclear buildup has rendered Cold War-era arms control models "obsolete." The announcement comes as the first time in more than half a century that the world's two largest nuclear arsenals have no legally binding limits.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Satellite images show Iran prioritizing missile repairs over nuclear sites

featured_image.name: Satellite images show strikes' impact on Iran nuclear sites

items.description:
New satellite imagery analyzed by the New York Times shows Iran has swiftly restored more than a dozen ballistic missile facilities damaged during last year's 12-day war with Israel and subsequent U.S. strikes, while making only limited progress at major nuclear sites that were targeted in June 2025.[1][2][3]

The finding, published Friday, coincided with the first round of indirect U.S.-Iran nuclear talks in Oman since the conflict, with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi describing the negotiations as "a good start" focused "exclusively" on the nuclear issue.[4][5]

items.title: Venezuela's political prisoners could be freed by next Friday

featured_image.name: Jailed Venezuelan protesters could all be free by next Friday, top ...

items.description:
Venezuela's National Assembly is on track to grant final approval to an amnesty law on Tuesday that could lead to the release of all political prisoners by February 13, according to Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez.

In a video shared on Telegram on Friday, Rodriguez announced that the Amnesty Law for Democratic Coexistence, which passed its first vote unanimously on Thursday, is expected to receive final approval next week. "We are optimistic that by next Tuesday or by Friday at the latest, everyone will be released," Rodriguez said.[1][2][3]

The legislation, proposed by interim President Delcy Rodriguez following the U.S. military capture of Nicolas Maduro on January 3, would grant clemency to those jailed for participating in political protests or criticizing public officials. It also would lift political candidacy bans on opposition figures, including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado, return seized assets, and cancel Interpol notices to allow exiles to return home.[4][5][6][7]

items.title: Expert warns Musk's orbital data center timeline is 'aggressive'

featured_image.name: Elon Musk's SpaceX applies to launch 1m satellites into orbit

items.description:
Elon Musk this week announced an ambitious plan to launch up to one million solar-powered satellites into orbit to serve as data centers for artificial intelligence, a proposal experts say faces enormous technical, financial, and environmental hurdles despite the billionaire's track record of disrupting industries.

The plan, detailed in a filing submitted to the Federal Communications Commission on January 30, came alongside the merger of SpaceX and Musk's AI venture xAI in a deal valued at $1.25 trillion. Musk has argued that Earth-based solutions cannot keep pace with AI's surging energy demands and that orbital infrastructure offers near-constant solar power without atmospheric interference.[1][2][3]
